Emerging multi-agent LLMs demand privacy-preserving edge deployment, yet current inference systems struggle with these collaborative workflows. Specifically, the memory-bound decode phase causes severe bus contention on unified memory architectures (UMA), paralyzing naive CPU-GPU co-execution. Furthermore, speculative decoding in multi-agent workloads faces extreme variance in drafting difficulty, alternating between complex reasoning and predictable structured generation. Compounded by frequent tool-induced stalls, this highly fragmented execution severely underutilizes hardware and defeats traditional static batching. We present EdgeAgent , a cross-layer inference system explicitly co-designed for edge UMA and multi-agent workloads. At the micro-architectural level, it bypasses rigid graph-compiler constraints to enable zero-copy UMA-aware tensor parallelism, utilizing asymmetric memory layouts to fully saturate both CPU and GPU compute units. At the scheduling level, it dynamically allocates draft budgets based on real-time sequence predictability to bound bandwidth waste. Concurrently, an asynchronous suspend-and-yield mechanism actively evicts stalled agents, ensuring continuous hardware saturation during unpredictable tool invocations. Extensive evaluations on an Apple M4 SoC demonstrate that the UMA-aware execution alone contributes a 1.29× speedup over batched speculative decoding. Adding the agent-aware scheduling lifts the full EdgeAgent system to a 1.77× speedup under extreme tool-use latencies. Keywords: On-device LLM inference, Multi-agent systems, Unified memory architectures, Speculative decoding † † cc-license: by 1. Introduction The application of large language models ( Brown et al., 2020 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2024 ; Gerganov, 2023 ) (LLMs) is increasingly shifting from monolithic chat interfaces toward coordinated multi-agent systems. In recent agent frameworks, such as LangGraph ( LangChain AI, 2026 ) and OpenClaw ( OpenClaw Team, 2026 ) , a common design choice is to decompose complex tasks into specialized roles and coordinate them through explicit orchestration mechanisms. With the enhanced capability of multi-agent systems, they start to take over more system access privileges, raising growing privacy and security concerns. This trend makes on-device LLM inference deployment increasingly important. However, existing LLM inference systems can hardly handle such multi-agent workloads on end-user devices efficiently. Most existing LLM inference systems ( Kwon et al., 2023 ; Qin et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2022 ) are primarily designed for cloud environments and multi-user workloads. These systems process hundreds of concurrent requests across multiple discrete GPUs, targeting high-throughput batching and multi-tenant isolation. Lacking awareness of fine-grained, intra-node memory contention, their hardware and workload assumptions render them highly inefficient when ported directly to edge devices. Conversely, existing edge frameworks (e.g., Llama.cpp ( Gerganov, 2023 ) , MLX ( Apple Machine Learning Research, 2023 ) ) primarily target single-user, single-request sequential inference. When confronted with collaborative multi-agent workloads which dynamically generate concurrent, highly fragmented requests on a single device, these monolithic edge systems lack the necessary orchestration, leaving available compute resources severely underutilized. The more balanced CPU-GPU computing capability on modern edge devices enables effective use of tensor parallelism (TP) to coordinate heterogeneous execution and fully utilize on-chip compute resources ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025a ; Li et al., 2025c ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025b ) . Modern edge systems-on-chip (SoCs) typically integrate powerful mobile GPUs and highly capable CPUs with advanced matrix extensions, such as ARMv9 Scalable Matrix Extension ( Arm Limited, 2021 ) (SME) in the Apple M4 ( Apple Inc., 2024 ) , forming a well-proportioned heterogeneous computing platform. TP ( Narayanan et al., 2021 ) , as a mainstream model parallelism technique, partitions LLM workloads (e.g., matrix multiplications) across multiple devices, making it suitable for distributing computation between CPUs and GPUs to speed up inference. During the compute-bound prefill phase, heterogeneous TP can fully exploit aggregated floating-point throughput by engaging both processing units simultaneously. However, during the decode phase, such CPU-GPU parallelism brings little performance gain under the shared unified memory architecture (UMA), since the decoding process is inherently memory-intensive and severely bounded by memory bandwidth. To mitigate the memory bound in the decode phase, recent systems improve arithmetic intensity through speculative decoding (SD) ( Li et al., 2025d ; Cai et al., 2024 ) . SD decouples generation into two stages: a lightweight draft model first proposes multiple candidate tokens, and the target model then verifies them in parallel, accepting the longest matching prefix. By amortizing target-model weight loading across multiple token verifications, SD reduces per-token bandwidth pressure and improves decode throughput. However, integrating these hardware-aware optimizations for multi-agent workflows into existing graph-based edge frameworks, such as MLX, exposes three critical systemic bottlenecks. First, implementing CPU-GPU lock-free TP on shared memory exposes the limitations of modern graph compilers ( Lattner et al., 2021 ; Ansel et al., 2024 ) . Standard directed acyclic graph (DAG) executors cannot safely express asynchronous, orthogonal memory mutations to a single shared tensor, forcing runtimes into eager synchronization which severely disrupts the graph optimization pipeline and explicit memory copies that negate the zero-copy benefits of UMA. Second, different agent tasks exhibit extreme variance in the difficulty of drafting (e.g., highly structured code synthesis vs. deliberate reasoning). As this drafting difficulty is related to the real-time context, traditional SD systems allocate a static draft length uniformly across all tasks. This inevitably results in the waste of limited memory bandwidth, which is frequently used to process rejected drafts. Third, agents frequently execute external tool calls ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) that incur out-of-system stall. When an agent stalls on a tool call, the runtime cannot dynamically redistribute its idle speculative budget to remaining active agents, failing to fully exploit the available compute capacity and degrading overall system performance on edge devices. To address these challenges, we propose EdgeAgent , a co-designed inference system explicitly tailored for edge UMA and concurrent multi-agent workflows. EdgeAgent adopts a cross-layer architecture featuring an agent-aware scheduling layer, which tightly couples real-time agent states and task predictability directly with the underlying UMA-aware execution layer. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions: • We design a UMA-aware execution layer with a zero-copy TP graph that adopts symmetric memory layouts to eliminate compiler overhead, together with optimized SME micro-kernels to jointly saturate heterogeneous edge compute units. • We design an agent-aware scheduling layer that dynamically allocates draft budgets based on real-time drafting difficulty, and employs an in-place suspend-and-yield mechanism to instantly reclaim computation slots during tool-induced stalls. • We implement and evaluate EdgeAgent on modern edge architectures using trace-driven, concurrent multi-agent workflows. Experimental results demonstrate that our system delivers substantial improvements in both global concurrent throughput and end-to-end task makespan compared to state-of-the-practice inference frameworks. 2. Background and motivation 2.1. LLM Inference Process Figure 1 . LLM autoregressive decoding process. As illustrated in Figure 1 , LLM inference proceeds in an autoregressive manner, generating tokens sequentially until an end-of-sequence (EoS) token is reached. To improve efficiency, the key and value representations from previous steps are cached in memory (i.e., the KV cache), allowing subsequent steps to avoid recomputing them. Based on this mechanism, the inference process can be divided into two stages: prefill and decode. The prefill stage processes the input prompt and constructs the initial KV cache. Since the prompt usually contains multiple tokens, this stage exhibits substantial parallelism. In contrast, during the decode stage, the model generates one token at a time. Each step consumes the existing KV cache, produces a new token, and appends the corresponding KV entries. In end-user settings, inference is typically performed on a single request, where each decoding step processes only one token. As a result, the decode stage becomes largely memory-bandwidth-bound, limiting hardware utilization. Furthermore, because decoding proceeds token by token, it often constitutes the dominant portion of the overall inference latency. 2.2. Multi-Agent Inference Workloads Figure 2 . Multi-Agent workload. Unlike traditional LLM applications functioning as chatbots for sequential queries, the adoption of LLMs is rapidly shifting to a collaborative, multi-agent system. This shift starts from ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , which integrates LLM’s internal reasoning with external tools to solve complex tasks. In such a paradigm, completing a single user request requires coordination among multiple specialized agents, each exhibiting different workload characteristics, as illustrated in Figure 2 . For instance, an Orchestrator agent serves as the central planner, processing extensive historical contexts to formulate strategies via complex reasoning. As these open-ended reasoning traces lack rigid structures, they are difficult to draft speculatively. In contrast, Worker agents handle concrete execution by translating these plans into structured executable code or rigid tool-use instructions. Driven by fixed syntactic templates, their outputs are highly structured and consequently much easier to draft. Moreover, as Worker agents must wait for responses from external tools (e.g., executing scripts or querying APIs), they incur severe execution stalls. Ultimately, the multi-agent workload exposes the inference engine to a highly fragmented execution mode, characterized by significant differences in drafting difficulty and unpredictable temporal blocking. This fundamentally differs from the assumption of continuous, homogeneous processing in traditional LLM serving ( Yu et al., 2022 ; Kwon et al., 2023 ) , posing challenges for efficient execution of inference systems. 2.3. Speculative Decoding Figure 3 . Task-dependent non-linear speedup of speculative decoding on edge UMA: accepted tokens ( τ \tau ) increase sub-linearly with draft length L L , while the end-to-end speedup increases first and then degrades due to rejection overhead. To mitigate the memory bandwidth bottleneck of autoregressive generation, speculative decoding (SD) decouples inference into a lightweight drafting phase and a parallel verification phase. In this paradigm, a small draft model predicts candidate token sequences that the massive target model subsequently verifies in a single forward pass. This design effectively amortizes the high memory latency associated with loading target model weights from main memory, as the memory-intensive target model is invoked only once per draft batch rather than sequentially for each token. However, the speedup achieved by SD scales non-linearly with draft length L L , and this pattern varies significantly across different tasks. As illustrated in Figure 3 , we conduct a pre-experiment on an Apple M4 SoC, deploying the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B model. We evaluate the acceleration profiles across two highly contrasting multi-agent workloads: deliberate reasoning (sampled from LongBench ( Bai et al., 2025 ) ) and highly predictable structured generation (sampled from MBPP ( Austin et al., 2021 ) ). Empirically, the speedup initially surges as memory traffic is amortized across more accepted tokens. The accepted token rate τ \tau increases sub-linearly with L L , and the end-to-end speedup peaks at L = 16 L=16 with a maximum speedup of 1.69 × 1.69\times on the Structured Output Task. Beyond this optimal length, the speedup diminishes rapidly and even degrades, driven by the surging probability of consecutive draft rejections. Critically, this non-linear behavior is task-dependent. Tasks with low drafting difficulty (e.g., structured output generation) tolerate longer draft lengths and achieve higher peak speedups, while hard reasoning tasks experience diminishing returns at shorter L L due to frequent token rejections. This implies that different sub-agents require distinct optimal draft lengths to maximize acceleration, as their drafting difficulties and token predictability vary significantly. Unfortunately, existing SD frameworks enforce a uniform draft length across all requests within a batch to simplify kernel execution, which further leads to resource misallocation. Driven by the significant differences in drafting difficulty across various multi-agent tasks (§ 2.2 ), this one-size-fits-all budget allocation brings two critical issues. On one hand, generating deep drafts for hard-to-draft reasoning tasks wastes shared memory bandwidth, as many candidate tokens are ultimately rejected. On the other hand, batch-level constraints truncate highly predictable tool instruction generation, limiting their maximum theoretical token-acceptance rates. 2.4. The Edge UMA Memory Wall Modern SoCs (e.g., Apple M4, Snapdragon X ( Qualcomm Technologies, Inc., 2023 ) ) feature unified memory architectures (UMA) and advanced tensor extensions. By abandoning discrete topologies, UMA allows the CPU and GPU to share a single physical memory pool and bus interface. Simultaneously, equipped with extensions like ARMv9 SME, modern CPUs now rival mobile GPUs in dense computation, even outperforming them at small batch sizes. Though this convergence supports zero-copy sharing of model weights across heterogeneous cores, it triggers memory contention. Specifically, during the prefill phase, high arithmetic intensity keeps the system compute-bound, allowing heterogeneous tensor parallelism (TP) to effectively aggregate compute power. However, in the decode phase, extremely small batch sizes shift the bottleneck entirely to memory bandwidth, fundamentally degrading the efficiency of hardware concurrency. Table 1 . This bandwidth wall explains why heterogeneous TP during the decode phase yields negligible end-to-end speedup, necessitating an agent-aware global co-scheduling paradigm to bypass the bottleneck. 2.5. Graph Compiler Limitations Beyond the hardware memory wall, realizing fine-grained device coordination is obstructed by existing software infrastructure. The modern deep learning ecosystem relies heavily on graph compilation as the foundational software for high-performance inference. This paradigm manifests through distinct paths across frameworks: PyTorch introduced ExecuTorch ( Meta PyTorch Team, 2023 ) for ahead-of-time (AOT) static graph serialization, whereas Apple’s native MLX defaults to global lazy evaluation to dynamically construct computation graphs at runtime. Despite these divergent implementations, both approaches transparently construct a global directed acyclic graph (DAG) of the program. Leveraging this intermediate representation, backend compilers can execute aggressive operator fusion and in-place memory lifecycle reuse, drastically reducing the framework overhead associated with per-operator scheduling. While graph compilation has achieved tremendous success in optimizing for standalone hardware backends, its underlying DAG abstraction exposes severe system-level limitations for fine-grained, heterogeneous TP across the CPU and GPU on edge devices. The core deficiency of modern graph compilers lies in their coarse, tensor-level dependency tracking, which inherently struggles to safely express the lock-free, concurrent mutation of a single shared physical buffer. Within edge UMA architectures, avoiding exorbitant memory copy overheads requires the CPU and GPU to perform orthogonal writes to different offset regions of a contiguous memory block. However, because the DAG tracks data hazards strictly at a tensor-level granularity, it is semantically blind to these disjoint sub-tensor boundaries and flags these orthogonal writes as severe data conflicts. Unable to semantically guarantee the safety of such non-overlapping mutations, the state machine of the graph executor resorts to a conservative over-protection strategy. It forcibly inserts coherence hardware fences across device boundaries, compelling the local graph execution to fall back into an eager synchronization mode. This semantic gap within the DAG implementation induces severe interleaved blocking among heterogeneous instruction sequences, significantly diminishing the parallel speedups gained from underlying operator partitioning. 3. EdgeAgent Design and Implementation Figure 4 . The architecture overview of EdgeAgent As shown in Figure 4 , EdgeAgent acts as a cross-layer inference system that couples the multi-agent workflows with the hardware-level physical constraints of edge UMA. Instead of processing requests uniformly, EdgeAgent disaggregates each request’s resource scheduling from overall execution to prioritize resource allocation to demand-critical requests and improve overall resource utilization. The architecture is organized into two collaborative layers, i.e. execution layer and scheduling layer. The UMA-aware execution layer (Section 3.1 ) provides a unified heterogeneous backend to maximize hardware saturation via: (1) A zero-copy TP computation graph, which features asymmetric memory layouts for heterogeneous processors, plus custom DAG barriers that bypass compiler overheads to enable lock-free tensor parallelism (Section 3.1.1 ). (2) SME micro-kernel optimizations, which combine instruction-level pipelining, cache-aware tiling, and dynamic work-stealing to maximize CPU efficiency (Section 3.1.2 ) . The agent-aware scheduling layer (Section 3.2 ) employs a dynamic global scheduler to maintain optimal hardware saturation via two mechanisms. First, to maximize throughput with limited draft slots, it dynamically allocates budgets toward highly predictable sequences using the Historical Accepted Length (HAL) as an indicator of drafting difficulty (Section 3.2.1 ).
